highlights: General Douglas MacArthur established GHQ SCAP in Tokyo on 2 October 1945, activating nine Special Staff Sections to supervise non-military occupation policies.
SCAP issued the 4 October 'Bill of Rights' directive, repealing the Peace Preservation Law, abolishing thought-control police, and freeing 507 political prisoners.
Prime Minister Prince Higashikuni's cabinet resigned en bloc on 5 October following SCAP's civil liberties directive, replaced on 9 October by Baron Kijuro Shidehara.
The four major Zaibatsu combines—Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Yasuda, and Sumitomo—agreed to voluntary dissolution plans transferring their holding company securities to a liquidation commission.
SCAP ordered the arrest of former Premier Hideki Tojo, his Pearl Harbor Cabinet, and approximately 300 suspected war criminals.
General MacArthur proclaimed U.S. Military Government in Korea on 7 September 1945, refusing recognition to domestic provisional regimes amid partition at the 38th parallel.
Japanese coal production plunged from 3.4 million metric tons in June 1945 to under 600,000 tons in October following the liberation of forced laborers.

sections.summary: Includes the title page, document documentation sheet, War Department transmittal memorandum, and general table of contents for the initial monthly summation.
sections.title: Front Matter

sections.summary: Executive summaries of SCAP organization, initial political and social reforms in Japan, economic stabilization and demilitarization, and civil administration in Korea.
sections.title: Part I: General

sections.summary: Details the establishment of GHQ SCAP in Tokyo, activation of nine Special Staff Sections, indirect control mechanisms via the Japanese Government's Central Liaison Office, and the administrative framework for Military Government in Korea.
sections.title: Section 1. Organization under SCAP

sections.summary: Summarizes political reforms including the 4 October 'Bill of Rights' directive, fall of the Higashikuni Cabinet and formation of the Shidehara Cabinet, dismissal of 4,800 thought-police officials, release of political prisoners, emergence of new political parties, and early war crimes arrests.
sections.title: Section 2. Political and Social Activities in Japan

sections.summary: Reviews the demilitarization of war industries, initial plans for dissolving Zaibatsu holding companies, legalization of trade unions, severe coal and food shortages, strict foreign trade and exchange controls, and the closure of 29 wartime colonial banks.
sections.title: Section 3. Economic Activities in Japan

sections.summary: Surveys early operations of U.S. Military Government in South Korea, the impact of division at the 38th parallel, replacement of Japanese personnel, emergence of dozens of political factions, critical coal shortages, and prevention of winter typhus epidemics.
sections.title: Section 4. Civil Administration in Korea

sections.summary: Covers government administration, political reorganization, legal affairs, public safety, and intelligence activities in Japan.
sections.title: Part II: Political

sections.summary: Details the operation of indirect administration through the Japanese Diet and Ministries, the fall of the Higashikuni Cabinet and formation of the Shidehara Cabinet, prefectural governorship shake-ups, early constitutional revision committees, proposed woman suffrage, and the emergence of competing political parties.
sections.title: Section 1. Government and Civil Administration

sections.summary: Reports the complete demobilization of the armed forces, abrogation of peace preservation laws, release of political prisoners, purge of 4,800 secret police, arrest orders for Tojo and 300 war criminals, and implementation of press censorship.
sections.title: Section 2. Legal, Public Safety and Intelligence

sections.summary: Comprehensive report on natural resources, industry, transportation, foreign trade, labor, communications, rationing and price control, and finance in Japan.
sections.title: Part III: Economic

sections.summary: Documents severe food deficits aggravated by September typhoon damage to rice crops, the establishment of authorized fishing zones amid fuel and net shortages, urban charcoal shortages, and a catastrophic drop in coal production following the liberation of forced laborers.
sections.title: Section 1. Natural Resources

sections.summary: Surveys industrial stagnation, authorization of monthly truck production, 24-hour shipyard repair operations, severe iron and steel declines due to coal shortages, textile deficits, plans to dissolve wartime control associations, and restrictions on scientific research including cyclotrons.
sections.title: Section 2. Industry

sections.summary: Assesses operational conditions across transportation sectors, noting relative railroad resilience despite passenger overcrowding, severe deterioration of motor vehicles, and the reduction of active merchant shipping to 908,000 gross tons allocated primarily to coastal coal and repatriation.
sections.title: Section 3. Transportation

sections.summary: Outlines foreign trade controls limiting imports to vital necessities paid by approved exports, reports identified export surpluses such as raw silk, details emergency coal exports to Korea and Hong Kong, and reviews the legacy of wartime military trading companies.
sections.title: Section 4. Imports and Exports

sections.summary: Covers labor procurement for Allied forces, projected unemployment of over four million, restoration of prewar protective labor standards, rebirth of independent labor unions under a unified federation, and violent strikes among liberated Korean and Chinese coal miners.
sections.title: Section 5. Labor

sections.summary: Details emergency rehabilitation of war-damaged telephone and telegraph networks for Allied use, censorship of international radio circuits, redistribution of seized military vacuum tubes, slow manufacturing recovery of communications equipment, and restrictions on electronics research.
sections.title: Section 6. Communications

sections.summary: Reports the breakdown of commodity distribution, reduction of the staple food ration to 294 grams, critical newsprint and textile shortages, pervasive black-market pricing up to 260 times official ceilings, and efforts to reform price control mechanisms.
sections.title: Section 7. Rationing and Price Control

sections.summary: Details fiscal distress, currency stabilization at ¥42 billion, closure and liquidation of 29 wartime colonial banks, impounding of gold and silver reserves, unsettled war damage insurance guarantees, and initial dissolution plans for the four major Zaibatsu combines.
sections.title: Section 8. Finance

sections.summary: Reports on public health, welfare administration, medical supplies, education reform, religious freedom, cultural preservation, and media liberalization in Japan.
sections.title: Part IV: Social Services

sections.summary: Surveys damaged hospital facilities, relief programs for over 83,000 persons, venereal disease control directives, emergency typhus prevention measures among repatriates, transfer of military medical stockpiles, and the delivery of relief supplies to Hiroshima.
sections.title: Section 1. Public Health and Welfare

sections.summary: Details educational demilitarization and teacher screening, abolition of the Religious Bodies Law, plans to separate State Shinto from the state, dissolution of the Domei news monopoly, and the introduction of democratic radio, film, and theatrical programs.
sections.title: Section 2. Education, Religion and Media of Expression

sections.summary: Surveys political developments, economic conditions, and social affairs under United States Army Military Government in South Korea.
sections.title: Part V: Korea

sections.summary: Details the establishment of direct U.S. Military Government, the impact of partition at the 38th parallel, purging of Japanese officials and police, intense rivalry among 54 political parties, the return of Syngman Rhee, and widespread hostility toward trusteeship.
sections.title: Section 1. Political

sections.summary: Reports the establishment of a free market in rice, severe fertilizer and fuel deficits caused by severed supplies from North Korea, emergency coal shipments from Japan, reorganization of railroads and communications, and strict financial controls.
sections.title: Section 2. Economic

sections.summary: Covers the reopening of secondary schools with Korean-language instruction, expansion of Military Government press and radio information services, creation of the Bureau of Public Health, mass immunization against typhus, and refugee relief operations at Fusan and Seoul.
sections.title: Section 3. Social

summary: Covering the foundational two months of the Allied occupation (September–October 1945), this initial summation records the establishment of General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (GHQ/SCAP) in Tokyo under General Douglas MacArthur and the simultaneous installation of U.S. Army Military Government in South Korea under the XXIV Corps. In Japan, SCAP instituted indirect governance through the Japanese cabinet and Diet while enforcing rapid demilitarization, dissolving the imperial military, and issuing the historic 4 October 'Bill of Rights' directive. That directive abolished thought-control police, repealed repressive statutes like the Peace Preservation Act, freed political prisoners, precipitated the collapse of the Higashikuni Cabinet, and initiated constitutional revision. The report portrays widespread economic paralysis across both territories: catastrophic coal deficits following the liberation of Korean and Chinese forced laborers, acute food shortages worsened by devastating September typhoons, uncontrolled black markets, and fiscal turmoil. In Korea, authorities confronted the crippling economic and political division along the 38th parallel, the rise of dozens of competing political factions, and popular resistance to allied trusteeship. For historians, the report provides invaluable baseline statistical surveys, structural blueprints of occupation administration, and candid accounts of early policy improvisation.
